name: Christian American Association

summary.text: The Christian American Association was incorporated in Houston in 1936 by Vance Muse to continue his campaign against the New Deal. Historian Michael Pierce describes it as the vehicle through which Muse, with Dallas Morning News writer William Ruggles's blessing, launched the 'right-to-work' campaign in the early 1940s; Pierce's testimony says Arkansas planters funded Muse's anti-strike campaign, and journalist Chris Kromm says the group was backed by Southern oil companies and Northeastern industrialists.

sources.title: The Origins of Right-to-Work: Vance Muse, Anti-Semitism, and the Maintenance of Jim Crow Labor Relations

facts.claim: Pierce writes that Muse visited Ruggles soon after his 1941 editorial and secured his blessing for the Christian American Association to launch a campaign to outlaw contracts requiring union membership; Ruggles suggested the 'Right-to-Work' name.
facts.quote: secured the writer's blessing for the Christian American Association to launch a campaign to outlaw contracts that required employees to belong to unions

sources.title: The Origins of Right-to-Work: Vance Muse, Anti-Semitism, and the Maintenance of Jim Crow Labor Relations

facts.claim: Pierce's 2023 testimony, as summarized by LAWCHA, says Arkansas planters funded Muse's campaign for a state anti-strike law and turned to him to pass what it calls the nation's first right-to-work law.
facts.quote: Arkansas planters funded Muse's successful campaign to enact a state "anti-strike" law

sources.title: Michael Pierce Testifies About the Origin of Right to Work

facts.claim: Labor Notes (Pierce) says the pre-packaged anti-strike law sold first in Texas, then Mississippi and Arkansas, making strikers rather than strikebreakers or management criminally liable for picket-line violence.
facts.quote: made strikers, not strikebreakers or management, criminally liable for picket-line violence

openQuestions: Site claim: 'funded by Southern planters and industrialists' is supported; 'Arkansas and Florida, 1944' is only partly supported (Arkansas yes; Florida and 1944 not in opened sources). Named individual donors to the association were not found; the Dixon 2007 Journal of Policy History article cited by the site was not opened.
